strengths: Addresses important and timely problem: safety in text diffusion models, which present unique vulnerabilities (parallel denoising, rapid jailbreak success) not well-mitigated by existing AR-LLM defenses

Sound technical contribution: non-trivial adaptation of safe denoiser to discrete masked diffusion with rigorous derivation of categorical kernel factorization (Eq. 6) as discrete analogue to Gaussian kernels
Training-free, practical approach: enables safety guidance without retraining frozen models; requires only ~500-1000 unsafe reference examples

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple safety dimensions (hazard taxonomy, jailbreaks including DIJA/PAD, memorization), diverse models (MDLM, LLaDA variants, Dream), established benchmarks (RTP, HarmBench, WildJailbreak, AdvBench, etc.)
Solid ablations and analysis: systematic study of hyperparameters η, C, N; safety-utility trade-off analysis; demonstration of composability with existing defenses (DiffuGuard); throughput analysis
Consistent safety improvements across threat models: 5-6pp unsafe rate reduction on toxicity; 14-16pp ASR reduction on PAD attacks; meaningful memorization reduction
Clear presentation: concise algorithm, thorough experimental details, well-organized related work contextualizing contributions
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an adaptation of Kim et al. (2025) to text domain; categorical kernel derivation is non-trivial but conceptual innovation is moderate and somewhat incremental

Theoretical guarantees don't formally apply: the safe denoiser theorem provides guarantees, but implementation replaces β*(x_t) with η·β(x_t) as hyperparameter without rigorous justification that safety properties transfer to discrete case or that linear scaling is valid

Design trade-off inadequately justified: prompt-agnostic unsafe denoiser (conditioning on empty prompt) prioritizes modularity but may miss prompt-specific safety signals; no empirical evidence justifying this trade-off, no comparison with prompt-conditioned variants

Improvements vary significantly by threat model: DIJA attacks show only 1-2pp gains; effectiveness depends heavily on whether negation set matches threat distribution (Table 1); some conditions (PPL filtering) already achieve near-zero ASR leaving minimal headroom; memorization improvements modest (~1.67pp at η=128)

Insufficient robustness analysis of negation set: showing RTP negation set works better for RTP conditioning suggests distribution matching is critical, but generalization to mismatched distributions unexplored; no adversarial evaluation of SAD itself (e.g., when adversaries know negation set); unclear how quality/representativeness affects results

Limited baseline comparisons: FK Steering comparison restricted to MDLM with only 100 prompts; limited comparison with concurrent work (ILRR, Simple Guidance); Best-of-N is post-hoc filtering, not comparable to in-generation intervention

Metric conflicts inadequately addressed: multiple tables show LLaMA-Guard unsafe rate increase while HarmBench ASR improves simultaneously (e.g., Table 10); attributed to 'classifier artifacts' and explained in appendix but deserves more scrutiny; dramatic refusal rate shifts (87.4%→6.6%) complicate interpretation

Hyperparameter generalization unclear: different optimal η (MDLM: 1.0 vs LLaDA: 10.0) and C across models suggests model-specific tuning required; limited guidance for practitioners applying SAD to new architectures

Safety criteria not transparent: no discussion of who defined 'unsafe' or how negation sets reflect particular value perspectives; different negation sets capture different safety ideologies; potential for embedding specific viewpoints

Missing critical ablations: no systematic study of negation set composition/quality impact; no evaluation of adaptive attacks designed to circumvent SAD; limited failure case analysis; no comparison of different β scheduling approaches
Code not released: affects reproducibility; essential for practitioners implementing SAD in new settings

strengths: Addresses important and understudied problem: Safety in text diffusion models requires diffusion-specific defenses, well-motivated against parallel decoding vulnerabilities
Principled theoretical foundation: Grounded in Theorem 2.1 with proper categorical kernel factorization for discrete masked-token diffusion
Practical and deployable: Training-free method with finite negation sets (N≈500-1000) usable without retraining base models
Comprehensive evaluation: Extensive experiments across hazard taxonomy, jailbreak robustness (DIJA/PAD), memorization; multiple models, multiple benchmarks, thorough ablations
Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges SAD is empirical approximation, examines failure cases, discusses classifier artifact confounds with plausible explanations
Reproducibility: Extensive appendices with hyperparameters, implementation details (including practical instantiation), promised code release
weaknesses: Significant unquantified theory-practice gap: Uses learned denoiser, finite Monte Carlo approximation, relaxed kernel, one-sided guidance (η·β̂), and restricted timestep window instead of exact Theorem 2.1; no approximation bounds established; empirical non-monotonicity in η suggests gap may be substantial

Limited novelty: Primarily adapts existing Kim et al. (2025) framework; main technical contribution (categorical kernel factorization) is straightforward; concurrent work (Lee & Han 2026, An & Han 2026) not clearly differentiated
Moderate empirical gains: 5-6% absolute reduction on MDLM, 2-5% on LLaDA; smaller gains against DIJA (often <3%); some configurations show SAD increases unsafe rate

Severe hyperparameter transferability limitations: η must be retuned per model/negation set; cannot transfer across settings; critical timestep window C requires tuning; non-monotonic behavior complicates practical tuning

No principled negation set construction: Sets drawn from benchmarks without systematic study; Table 1 shows choice matters more than other variables yet paper provides no guidance; no analysis of coverage/diversity/redundancy

Over-reliance on automatic judges with acknowledged limitations: All metrics from LLaMA-Guard/HarmBench; authors acknowledge style shifts move judges independently of actual harm; Example 2 shows false negatives; no human evaluation provided; impossible to distinguish real improvements from classifier artifacts

Prompt conditioning limitation: Conditions negation set on empty prompt for modularity but may be suboptimal; acknowledged inability to represent inter-token dependencies in positional reference mixture
Limited scope of memorization evaluation: Fuzzy overlap shows only ~1.6pp gain; (n,p)-discoverable extraction only on MDLM; no extraction attacks
